title: Block close: letters to you
hook: the letters were written to real churches, and churches still read them as addressed to them
tomorrow: a short old book opens at a fork in the road. which way?

segments.voice: The last page of Romans thanks Phebe, Priscilla and Junia by name, beside lines that limit women, read differently by different churches. Co-workers in Christ. Now the last page of this whole stretch of letters.
screen: `CO-WORKERS IN CHRIST.` → `THE LAST PAGE OF THE LETTERS.`

segments.voice: Some people write a letter to their future self and seal it, or schedule an email to land years from now. The person who opens it won't quite be the person who wrote it. Romans has an address on it: "To all that be in Rome, beloved of God, called to be saints." Real people, in a real city, waiting for news. Nobody in that room was writing to a stranger far down the road. So who is that letter addressed to now?
screen: `A LETTER TO YOUR FUTURE SELF.` → `TO ALL THAT BE IN ROME.` → `ADDRESSED TO WHOM, NOW?`

segments.voice: Look back over this stretch: a scribe named Tertius, hymns caught on the page, household codes read in context, a page of hellos full of co-workers. Every letter went to someone else first. Romans to Rome. Philemon to one man, about one brother. So how do churches read other people's mail? The letters open that door themselves. First Corinthians is written "Unto the church of God which is at Corinth," and then the address widens: "with all that in every place call upon the name of Jesus Christ our Lord, both theirs and ours." Every place. Colossians asks to be passed along: "when this epistle is read among you, cause that it be read also in the church of the Laodiceans." A letter for one town, read aloud in the next. Churches have kept doing that. Read in worship, the letters are heard as addressed to whoever is sitting there. That doesn't erase Corinth. Reading in context means remembering who opened the letter first. Reading as if to you means letting it open you too. Both at once. And tomorrow a new block begins: the saints and teachers who came after, in their own words.
screen: `EVERY LETTER HAD A FIRST READER.` · `IN EVERY PLACE, THEIRS AND OURS.` · `READ IT ALSO IN LAODICEA.` · `CONTEXT AND YOU, BOTH AT ONCE.` · then, large: `READ AS IF TO YOU.`

segments.voice: Write a few lines to your future self, on paper if you can. Open the way the letters do: who it's from, who it's to, a word of thanks. Then add one thing you hope that future self still remembers.
Block close. The end of the letters read in their own words: mail to real churches, still read as if written to whoever opens it.
Your line: read as if to you. Corinth got it first, and the address kept widening. A block, closed.

fork.setup: your grandfather reads you a letter his own father wrote him long ago and says, 'this is for you now too.' a cousin says that's silly; it was his letter. how do churches read Paul's letters?

fork.reveal: 1 Corinthians widens its own address to 'all that in every place', and Colossians asks to be read in the next town. churches read the letters as if to them, without erasing the first readers.

chat.says: senior english: write a letter to future me, opened in 10 yrs. feels so cringe. what do i even put?
options: Write it like Paul's letters: who it's from, who it's to, thanks first. Real mail still reaches later readers.
Keep it vague. Letters meant for later can't be personal, or nobody else could ever read them.
Skip the thanks and names. Old letters only matter for their big ideas, not the people in them.
chat.meaning: The letters were real mail with names and thanks, and churches still read them as if addressed to them. Being personal is what lets a letter travel.

Corinth.meaning: a Greek city whose church received Paul's letters

Laodiceans.meaning: the church at Laodicea, named in Colossians 4:16

Philemon.meaning: Paul's short letter to one man about one brother

Tertius.meaning: the scribe who wrote Romans down
